chapters.html:
All he sees is red.

Burning flames. Thick, ashen smoke. The ebb and flow of black tide. 

Where the brilliant sun once stood, a blood red half-sun hangs, painting the blue sky in shades of crimson. The scorch of flames desiccates the land, and lush fields, once filled with tall green grass and blooming wildflowers, crumble away in the wind. A lone poppy floats by, its pink petals singed black as it flutters into the ruins of the bustling village square. 

Regardless of the singing heat, a bone-chilling ache wracks his body. Hot, thick ash burns his nostrils and bitter bile floods his mouth as he kneels wretched on the cracked earth. All around him are the human screams of those trapped in the rubble punctuated by the shrill shrieks of black tide monstrosities. 

A boy stumbles towards him, his body warped and face mutilated beyond recognition. “Help… H-Help me…!” He gasps out as he stumbles on the broken remains of another and crumbles onto the earth without another sound. 

A few feet away lies his mother, her eyes glassy and without breath, the rise and fall of her chest ceased. Half of her body has already corroded away, replaced by sweltering red and black that eats away at her tender flesh. 

Tears fall in a flurry as he chokes down yet another sob. He wants to scream, wants to yank himself from the floor yet his body doesn’t react. He can’t move, an invisible force presses him down and keeps him in place. All he can do is watch as the destruction unfolds, as the last remnants of his home crumble away right before his eyes. 

A monster cloaked in black approaches, its shattered greatsword glowing and stained with the blood of thousands. The metal mask obscuring its features glints red from flame. It remains silent, not a singular word uttered as it slowly comes to a stop in front of him.

And like it always does, how this nightmare always ends, it mechanically raises its arms and slashes down. 

Phainon gasps awake.

His fingernails shred into his thin bed sheets, and his body is drenched in cold sweat. The corner of his eyes burn with unshed tears as he lays there, staring blankly at the ceiling with his chest rapidly rising and falling.

He presses his arm over his face, smearing tears as he tries to regulate his breathing. A laugh bubbles in his parched throat, and though he tries, he fails to hold it in. A wretched cry springs free from his lips which soon turn to ragged coughs. 

Better to laugh like a madman than start sobbing like a toddler, he thinks absentmindedly. One inspires fear, the other pity. He does not want to be pitied. 

His hand shoots out as he fishes for the pills hidden in his cabinets. Sleep inducers. He haphazardly dumps a few in his mouth and swallows them dry, feeling as they slowly crawl down his throat without any suitable lubrication. For a moment, he regrets it, but he can’t be bothered to stand up to retrieve water, even as they burn and dissolve, astringent and bitter. 

This is what he gets for not taking them. He tried for Hyacine’s sake, couldn’t say no to her as she pleaded for him to stop. By titans, he tried. She told him it would hurt him in the long run, and yes, he’s well aware, but how can he when they’re the only way he can rest properly through the night? Without them, he’s plagued by… by this . The same nightmare on repeat over and over and over. 

This is divine punishment. He knows it to be. 

Aedes Elysiae is no more, yet somehow, he’s still here. Alive, though he doesn’t feel like it at times. 

The one final survivor. The boy that picked up the blade and slaughtered his loved ones as they warped into what they feared the most. The only person that the black clad swordsman allowed to live. 

Allowed. That’s a distinction that needs to be made. 

Though he tries to push against it, the flood of memories is unrelenting, and he falls back, submerged in the chaos of the past and the simpler times. He twists and turns, unable to find a single comfortable position. 

“Stop—” he says as he presses his hands to his ears and screws his eyes shut. “Stop…”

It’s a futile effort. He knows it to be, yet he still tries. 

His mother loved to bake, their quaint little home constantly filled with the smell of freshly baked bread and sweet pastries, but he can’t remember her smile nor her voice when she called out for him to stay safe and return home before dark. He can only see the last moments of her life, the empty of her eyes as she slowly corroded away. 

He can’t remember his father’s face, but he knows it to be aged by the sun, stern yet kind. His father loved the skies, pointing at the twinkling stars as he explained the twirling constellations that represented love, good fortune, and prosperity, but those memories draw a blank when he tries to recall. All he sees is crimson blood pouring out of the wound in his broad back as he protects his son with his body.  

With each passing day, his childhood fades away, even as he desperately tries to grasp at it, to keep it locked tightly in his heart so he can revisit the times when he was free and happy. Even Cyrene’s face is a blur. His childhood friend whom he cherished with all his soul, her presence always brought the sweetest warmth. All he can recall now is the gold splashing out of the jagged blade lodged in her chest, her blood-stained lips quirking up in a sad smile as she reached out and said her goodbyes.

“Stop!” He screams as he slams his fists against the mattress. “Stop… Please—” He swallows, nearly chokes, and dumps a few more pills down his throat. “Please…” 

In his heart, he knows. As his memories continue to slip and fade, as he forces each day and trudges through the unknown with a forced smile plastered onto his face, the further he drifts away from who he once was.

The smiling young boy who danced with his friends through fields of wheat is no more. In his place is a man who can barely remember anything but the flames and the screaming and the vile stench of death. 

He is the heir given the mission of deliverance. The one to usher in the new era and bring new light to a ravaged and torn Amphoreus. 

That’s all there is to Phainon of Okhema. 

***

When he wakes up, it’s halfway through lucid hour. 

Oh, no. Titans no. This can’t be happening. 

Stumbling to his feet, he scrambles to get ready, ignoring the pounding headache and the dryness of his mouth as he haphazardly slides on his armor. He grabs his bottle of pills and stuffs them into his pocket before rushing out of his house. 

He’s late. So very late. Mydei has probably already left without him. 

Great. What an amazing start to their first mission together.

Luckily for him, Mydei hasn’t yet left. Phainon spots blonde hair and familiar scarlet markings as he dashes towards the gates that separate Okhema from the untamed wilderness and the dark of the evernight. 

As always, the prince stands there like he owns the place, his arms crossed and expression indifferent as he gazes calmly at Phainon’s direction. His golden eyes narrow in wait as a soft breeze rustles his spiky hair and jingles his golden ornaments. He looks equal parts threatening, equal parts stunning, not that Phainon would ever admit that part out loud. 

Apprehension grows in his chest, its roots carving a home in his heart. The flower blooms, bloodied petals unfurling, sustained by the anxiety that plagues his every movement. He swallows down the unease and marches forward with greater force. 

They’ve been assigned a mission together in a remote fishing village a few days walking distance from Okhema. The chief requested their assistance with some strange happenings. In the last few months, many villagers have disappeared without a trace and an oppressive aura blankets the area every few days, smothering the village in a dark and toxic miasma. 

Aglaea also requested they clear out any titankin they encountered along the way. A two-in-one mission. Phainon’s been itching to kill monsters, to relieve the frustration that’s been building up for the past few weeks, so he’s excited to finally get the opportunity. It’s his favorite pastime, to lose himself to the adrenaline rush of battle and let free of his bothersome thoughts and become one with his greatsword. 

“You’re late,” Mydei says the moment Phainon’s in hearing range. 

“Yes,” he replies, out of breath, as he runs his hand through slick moonlight hair. “My apologies. I lost track of time.”

Mydei’s sharp eyes lazily trace over his form, scanning and seeing .

Phainon resists the urge to bolt. Instead, he gives a bright smile and says, “We should get going.” 

Thankfully, Mydei doesn’t question him, only picks up his bag and begins his way out. 

Though they’re to return in probably no more than a few days, Phainon bids a silent goodbye to Okhema. With each step, the wilderness grows thicker, and the sky grows darker. He slowly trails behind Mydei, ensuring a suitable distance between them. He has no desire to move closer.  

Mydei strides forward in confidence, his gait steady as the muscles in his back ripple with each step. Each movement is calculated, smooth with a charisma that inspires attention and turns heads. Already, Phainon feels a little irked. He shouldn’t feel this way, but his head hurts and his armor feels a little tight, strapped against his skin.  

With all due respect, Aglaea must have been possessed when she decided to pair them together. 

“I can handle the mission alone,” Phainon had told her only for the goldweaver, glowing and ever elegant, to shake her head, her blonde curls bobbing in rhythm. 

With a twirl of her hand, she had responded, “Mydeimos is new to Okhema yet a powerful asset. I believe there’s a lot of good that will come from the two of you learning to work together.” 

Her tone of voice was final, unwavering, and Phainon couldn’t find it in himself to try to argue. Once she made up her mind, she wouldn’t budge, and he was only wasting his effort. He supposed it was true, though he was rather loath to admit it, that Mydei was now a part of the flame-chase journey and had to be shown the ropes.  

Even so, that doesn't mean he had to be excited about it. 

Ten days and ten nights of battle. That’s how they met, and their relationship thus far amounted to, well, fighting. The flames of competition stoked and burned, he found himself wanting to best Mydei at everything. 

But he doesn’t know Mydei at all. They speak through their fists and weapons, never with words. In the two months since Mydei’s arrival, they’ve barely had a thorough conversation with how busy Mydei has been sorting through matters regarding his people. Settling down in a new city as refugees is never easy, even worse how Okhema and Castrum Kremnos are enemy city-states and have been for millennia. 

And Phainon doesn’t quite like the way his chest squeezes whenever he looks at the other man. It’s a strange feeling he can’t quite grasp. Not quite jealousy, not quite admiration, though he does find himself staring Mydei’s body for longer than he should. 

His head begins to ring once more. He slowly rubs at his temples. 

Mydei turns and regards him with those infuriating golden eyes. “You better not drag me down, Deliverer. Speed it up. We’re not here to sightsee.”

Irked, Phainon sprints towards Mydei until they’re side to side and says, “As if. This is what, your first mission? You’re the rookie here.”

“I’ve led armies. This is no more than child’s play,” Mydei responds as he continues to stride on without sparing Phainon another glance.  

Phainon’s eye twitches.  

The hours go by as they slowly trek through the dark of the wilderness. The further they get from Okhema, the darker the sky becomes and the quieter the surroundings. The evernight looms, and the silence is suffocating. No words are exchanged, but Mydei does glance over his every so often. 

For once in his life, Phainon has nothing to say. Normally, he’s one to speak his mind. After all, he’s been told his ability to talk nonstop is a talent in itself. He almost wants to laugh at that notion. If only they knew why. 

He doesn’t have anything to discuss with Mydei. What is he supposed to say when he barely knows this man? A man so unlike himself that it’s almost a crime to even compare them. They only speak through battle. That’s all. 

The trees grow thicker and the terrain rockier. Phainon pushes a branch out of his way, resisting the urge to snap it off the tree entirely. 

Evernight looms, and they set up camp in a quiet, hidden location. They eat a quiet dinner of packed rations, tasteless but filling. Mydei offers to take the first shift, and Phainon doesn’t have it in him to argue. 

With Mydei here, he can’t afford to show any signs of weakness. The Kremnoans—Mydei— scorn weakness and any kinks in his armor will be exploited. After all, he has his image to protect and maintain. He can’t let Amphoreus down, can’t allow himself to crack. 

And he knows. By titans, he knows he needs to relax lest he humiliate himself before the mission even begins. This is far from his first yet he’s acting as if it is while Mydei remains stoic, unbothered. He can’t afford to make a fool of himself in front of Mydei. Not now, not ever.

His throat constricts. He can’t help when his eyes flit over to the man beside him. Mydei stares back at him, those sharp golden eyes bright in the dark of the evernight. 

***

After the initial and rather uncomfortable day of silent, empty forests, they stumble upon groups of titankin roaming around the ruins of what evidently used to be a grand temple. As usual, the torch of competition is lit, and they both spring into action. A simple game of who could dispatch the most monsters in a set amount of time, it ends in a tie, though Phainon posits he won because Mydei stole one of his kills at the last minute. 

“You were too slow to take the last hit,” Mydei drawls, amused. “That’s on you, Deliverer. Don’t be a sore loser.”

“I gave it to you out of pity,” Phainon shoots back. “If anyone’s the sore loser, it’s you.” 

“Hmph.” The barest hint of a smile. Mydei’s blonde hair is in disarray, and he’s breathing heavily, but he looks content in a way Phainon has never seen before and his crimson marks seem to glow in the dim light. It makes Phainon’s chest hurt. A stray thought floats through his head that Mydei is most alive in battle and most beautiful too.

Time flies as they continue to slice down titankin after titankin, and they make it to the village without another hitch. It’s a peaceful place, rather unremarkable by all means. On the outskirts of any major city-state, outside the hustle and bustle, they should have been safe from the black tide, isolated from the rest of Amphoreus, yet that’s not the case. 

Phainon looks around. He’s never heard of this place before, has never even seen it on a map, but it strikes a chord in his chest, and he swallows down the unease. 

The village buildings are simple, humbly made of wood and clay brick. In the center, there’s a single central worship temple crafted of stone, greying and crumbling at the edges. Wild, leafy foliage climbs the aging structure, wrapping around the decaying pillars and snaking into the pediment. 

A creaky wooden dock leads out to sea with small wooden boats strung along the shore. Large fields of lush grass dance gently in the wind, framing the village.

Mydei bends down, his fingers tracing over dusty wood. Runes are carved into every corner and they seem to be blessings to Phaguosa asking for a fruitful, bountiful harvest and safety in the open seas.  

With each passing moment, the weight on Phainon’s chest grows heavier. This place reminds him so much of Aedes Elysiae. Even the air, floral yet tinged salty from the ocean waves, is very much the same.  

He sees a group of children running around, all smiles and giggles as they chase each other regardless of the gauntness of their cheeks and the tears in their thin tunics. When they spot the two of them, they pause, large eyes gazing in wonder, hands waving in the air. 

Phainon grins and waves back. 

There’s a little girl in pigtails, smaller than the rest, with a gap in her two front teeth. In her arms is a torn teddy bear, and she has dirt smeared on her cheek, but her smile is sweet and her eyes glitter as she dashes off.

The village chief calmly waits outside his residence. Initially, he’s shocked to see the two of them but recovers quickly with a warm greeting. He brings out refreshments of house-made wine as they discuss the details of the disappearances and the strange weather occurrences. 

Mydei only pretends to drink, his golden eyes roaming over the dark liquid, a pinch to his eyebrows. When Phainon goes to take his first sip, Mydei yanks it away from him, much to the shock of both the village chief and Phainon himself, only to calmly state that they cannot work inebriated. 

“My apologies for any offense,” the chief says with a small bow. His expression, though lined with age, remains light and carefree, as if he isn’t the captain weathering a great storm. “I did not mean any harm. It is our code to treat guests with utmost hospitality. This sea-salt grape wine is our specialty.” 

They are then politely shown to their lodgings. Unfortunately, they’re to reside in the same room as the village currently doesn't have the resources for another. 

Phainon takes it graciously. He understands what it’s like, living in a small village that has to scrounge every little bit to survive. It’s a simple lifestyle, far different from that of the major city-states enshrined with large marble pillared temples, decadence evident in every corner. 

Here, there’s only the farming fields, the ever challenging weather especially due to the evernight, and a strong will to survive that binds the community together. He’s surprised that crops are still able to grow. Sunlight doesn’t exist here, far away from Kephale’s neverending dawn, only artificial light created through magical means held in metallic lamps. 

Mydei looks around, his brow furrowing as he takes in the surroundings. His eyes continue to trail the runes carved in every corner and the brittleness of the wooden furniture in the small space. 

From earlier, Phainon already feels unsettled, but he pushes it down until Mydei approaches him, and in a low whisper, says, “Something isn’t right here.”

“You’ve been on edge since we’ve gotten here,” Phainon says. “Are the lodgings not to your liking, your highness?”

Mydei shakes his head and says, “Don’t eat or drink anything, and keep an eye out for any anomalies. There’s no reason why a village like this should be able to persist in Amphoreus’ current climate without any outside help. Aglaea has never heard of this place, nor has anyone else. That is all.” 

***

The ensuing days go by slowly. They explore the area in an attempt to find clues about the miasma, where it’s coming from and what it’s made of only to turn up empty-handed. There are no titankin roaming the village, but there are some scraps of black tide monstrosities that wash ashore every so often.

Mydei approaches with caution, convinced there’s something deeply off about the village and its inhabitants. He warns Phainon repeatedly not to eat anything, shoving at him a stash of rations, nutrient bars that he’s brought. Uptight and duty focused, there’s not a moment where the prince doesn’t look tense, ready to jump into combat at a moment’s notice. 

Yet, somehow, Phainon manages to rope Mydei into playing along with the children. It’s later in the day, past dinner, when they gather in the grass fields. 

Surrounded by so much laughter and giggling, Mydei looks like a fish out of water. He sits cross legged with Phainon beside him as the children scramble around, plucking flowers by their stems. A cool breeze rustles the grass and muses their hair. 

“Relax a little, will you?” Phainon elbows him. “We aren’t in battle.”

“I am very relaxed,” Mydei says stiffly. 

“Uh huh, and my blood is red,” Phainon quips.  

Mydei narrows his eyes but doesn’t respond. The veins in his arm pop from strain, and his back stays ramrod straight. 

Of course he’d be like this. Phainon doesn’t even find himself shocked by Mydei’s behavior, but he’s not about to let it dampen his mood. Watching the kids running around with wide smiles on their faces, he’s brought back to the times when he and Cyrene would play in the fields together. He would always try to find the weirdest, most outlandish looking flowers, bright neon and strange spiky petals, while Cyrene favored the pretty, dainty ones painted in sweet pinks with soft, rounded petals. They would thread the flowers together to make crowns, spending the entire afternoon grinning under the bright sun. 

With a brilliant smile, a little girl pops up to Mydei and hands him two flowers, a pure white lily and a blood red poppy. 

Mydei quietly thanks the girl, and she happily bounces off to collect more. He holds them in his hand yet does nothing except stare down at them in silence. For a warrior like him, he must be unaccustomed to such fleeting fragility. 

“You make the crown like this,” Phainon says as he leans over to pluck the flowers out of Mydei’s hands, surprising the other. He scoots closer to Mydei until their thighs nearly touch before continuing on, “You place the flowers side by side and knot the stem.” 

“I’m surprised you know how to make them,” Mydei says as he watches Phainon loop the stems together. 

Phainon smiles, tight at the corners. “I used to make them all the time when I was younger. Back then…” His voice trails off, and his eyes dim. His wandering thoughts threaten to pull him under so he clears his throat and says, “You also want to make sure the knots are tight or else the crown will fall apart.”

The children continue to bring them flowers, and Phainon fashions them into crowns of various sizes. To his surprise, Mydei tries to create his own following Phainon’s instructions. His attempts are clumsy but endearing nonetheless. 

With the first crown complete, Phainon leans in and places it atop Mydei’s head, admiring his handiwork. Confused, Mydei gazes back at him, his eyes a little wider than usual. His hand twitches, and for a moment, it seems like he’s going to pluck the crown off. It’s dark out with only a singular lamp as lighting, but the prince’s ears seem pink. 

The red and white petals mesh well with Mydei’s blonde, red-tipped hair and bring out the orange flecks in his eyes. Pretty. Neck up, Mydei looks like a beautiful flower nymph, one straight out of the fairy tales his mother used to read him.

“It suits you,” Phainon says with a satisfied nod. His chest feels a little strange, but he pays it no mind. 

Mydei pretends to not have heard him. Instead, he fiddles with the stems in his hand until one of them snaps. 

A boy skips up to Mydei, his curious eyes trailing the deep crimson covering Mydei’s chest and arms. “Mister Mydei… what are these markings?” 

“Interesting, aren’t they?” Phainon says. 

“They look like fire… like the bonfires we have sometimes!”

Mydei sets down his half-made flower crown. He pauses as he attempts to formulate an answer, eventually settling with, “These marks represent my existence. They are proof that I survived.” 

A bunch more kids gather around, eyes wide as they stare at the jagged crimson. 

“That’s so cool! I want to be strong like you when I grow up, mister Mydei!” another kid exclaims. 

Mydei ruffles the boy’s hair. “You are already strong. Be proud of your resilience, child.”

The boy tilts his head in confusion before nodding enthusiastically, “Thank you, mister Mydei!”

“I have a tattoo too,” Phainon pipes up. “Not as cool as his, but I think it’s pretty nice.” 

In an instant, all attention is on him. Even Mydei stares in his direction.  

Phainon clears his throat. He should have expected that, but it doesn’t stop the heat from travelling to his cheeks. 

“It’s a sun,” he says as he slowly unclasps his choker to show the marking hidden beneath—the bright yellow sun covering the entire side of his neck.

He feels golden eyes on him. Mydei is staring intensely at his tattoo, his expression unreadable. Phainon starts to feel a little self-conscious, but he shakes it off. 

“Sun?” a boy asks, eyes wide. “What’s that?” 

“Mm… It fills the sky. Blinding to look at but warm. Feels like a hug,” Phainon says. It doesn’t exist anymore. 

“Like lamps?” a boy asks. 

Phainon’s eyes soften. “Yes, like that but much bigger.” 

“My daddy said the lamps are made from something called…” the kid frowns. “Alc… something… Is the sun made of that too?”

“Magic!” another kid grins widely. “Not alchemy!”

“No, that’s not right!” the little girl shakes her head fervently as she clutches onto her teddy bear. “Mama told me the lamps hold fairies!” 

“Fairies?”

“They help us in exchange for friendship!” the girl defends. “They defend us from the outside and keep us safe!”

Phainon blinks. “The outside?” 

“Mama tells me we can’t leave …” the little girl says with a small frown. “It’s safer here, dangerous outside.”

Of course the children are ignorant to the happenings of Amphoreus. There’s no need to terrify them with the truth, not only to protect them but to also keep the smiles on their faces. Phainon understands, but the situation is dire and only grows worse with the passing days. 

His hands fiddle with his choker as he clasps it back in place. He’s not too sure what possessed him to show off the accursed tattoo on his neck. 

Beside him, Mydei shifts. “Here,” he says as he holds out his own flower creation and leans closer. Phainon’s breath catches in his throat when the crown is placed on his head. 

“Thank you, Mydei,” Phainon grins as he runs his fingers through the soft flowers. “Not bad for a first try.” 

Mydei gives a quick nod before turning away. 

For the rest of the night, they run around with the children and indulge in stories. They listen to the kids speak of their wishes and hopes for the future. As the night goes on, Mydei’s expression grows softer and his voice mellower. His lips quirk up into the barest of a smile, and Phainon finds he can’t look away. His heart skips a beat when Mydei looks over at him. 

There’s a stray piece of grass in Mydei’s hair from where they laid down earlier. Phainon finds himself leaning forwards. He reaches out, the tips of his fingers brushing against Mydei’s warm cheek.

“You have a piece of grass in your hair,” Phainon says softly. He holds it up. “See?” 

Mydei scoffs at him, but there’s no venom. It brings a smile to Phainon’s lips. Maybe this mission won’t be so bad after all. 

***

The sky burns crimson. The roar of flames and the static of black tide overwhelms all sense. Disarray paints every corner, and black tide monsters, many of whom were once villagers themselves, shred through any remaining life. 

Amidst the burning red, the ash and the smoke, a little girl smiles. In her arms is her favorite stuffed toy. 

“Mama…” the girl says, reaching out to the monster that was once her mother. Half of the woman’s body has been warped, transformed into the telltale metal plating of black tide monstrosities. 

“No! Get away!” Phainon yells, his legs pinned beneath rubble. His fingernails dig into the earth  as he tries to pull himself free, ignoring the searing pain in his thighs. He’ll tear his legs off if he has to. “Run! Hide! Leave! No… No—”

Blood splatters and lands warm on his cheek. Phainon’s eyes widen, his golden pupils constricting into pinpricks. A shrill shriek rips through his throat. 

The teddy bear lays bloodied on the scorched earth. 

***

There’s nothing left. The black tide had claimed every last soul, tearing apart those who had been inflicted by the miasma for too long. An experiment. The entire village had been contaminated from the slow trickle of black tide that seeped through the earth from the alchemical atrocities committed in the vast network of underground tunnels below. 

That’s what this fishing village became. A testing ground for a cult that worshipped the black tide. A group of heretics that believed they could harness the evil for themselves and become the new gods of Amphoreus. The chief had been one of those very heretics, but as for everyone else… They were only innocent people going about their lives with hope that through perseverance, they could thrive and live freely. 

The cult picked a prime area. Isolated enough for no one to notice their destruction. The very same as Aedes Elysiae. Only this was the work of living, breathing humans and not the warped, masked spectre. 

They wanted the golden blood of a Chrysos Heir to use for their heinous experiments and that was their downfall. To outsiders, there is no village in this area, only a barren spot of untouched nature, blocked off by magical barriers. 

Phainon stares blankly at the smoking rubble, the crumbled remains of what used to be townhouses and farm buildings. Not a single shred of foliage remains. The ground is cracked and splattered with black ash and crimson blood. 

There’s a deep crater in the center of the village, what was once the gathering area, where the facilities harboring human experimentation had self-detonated to hide evidence. Situated beneath the village in hidden tunnels, it had been difficult to infiltrate and much more difficult to navigate. 

The wind blows and brings with it thick, ashy soot. He chokes, wincing as he covers his mouth and nose only to be inundated with the stench of iron. 

His thighs burn yet he hobbles up to the bloodied, torn teddy bear and places it in his pocket. 

He failed them. He was supposed to protect them. They were counting on him. 

“Deliverer,” Mydei says. His expression remains flat as his eyes roam the premises, searching for any survivors but coming up with nothing. All the villagers had either perished in the explosion or had been transformed into monsters, cut down by Mydei’s merciless fists. 

Deliverer. The name falls freely from Mydei’s lips, mocking and slicing through his already bloodied flesh. That word, that accursed wretched curse of a word, is equal to a thousand cuts, and Phainon laughs miserably. 

He knows the truth now, has known it for years, but only now does it settle. He’s always been a mockery. He has never been a hero. 

Aglaea is wrong to trust him. 

***

With the village leveled, there’s little they can do but seek refuge elsewhere. 

Mydei wraps Phainon’s wounds and carries him on his back. Already, the prince has been healed of his injuries, looking brand new as if nothing had happened. Unchanged by the passage of time. 

Phainon, on the other hand, can barely walk, can barely even keep himself awake long enough to string together a sentence. He floats in and out of consciousness. The stinging in his chest, and the weight of the bloodied teddy bear in his pocket keeps him awake, but the despair pulls him down under. He doesn’t know if he cries or if he screams, but Mydei doesn’t speak a word. 

He’s lost track of time. When he opens his eyes once more, he’s laying on a bed inside of what looks to be an inn room. 

Mydei hovers over him and says, “I will go out to get us some supplies. Get some rest.” 

It sounds like an excuse to leave. He wonders if it’s because Mydei can’t stand the nauseating sight of him. He must look pitiful. 

Already, Mydei has stripped him of his shredded, ruined armor. It lays in a heap in the corner of the room. He’s in light cotton robes with his wound newly wrapped. 

The saturated light of the nightstand lamp burns his eyes, and he turns it off. The robes feel scratchy against his feverish skin, and the blankets smother him. His thighs ache with each movement, bruised he’s sure, and the gash in his chest, though shallow, stings with every breath he takes. It’s bearable and helps distract him from all else. 

Slowly, he makes his way to the bathroom and stares at himself in the mirror. 

He looks terrible. His lip is split, and his eyes reflect nothing, a deep abyss of dull blue. He looks every bit pathetic as he feels. 

In a fit of rage, he slams his fists onto the counter and screams.

Chapter Notes

Hi everyone!! I ended up splitting the first chapter into two because I realized that the flow of the story made more sense this way. This fic will end up as 3 chapters instead of 2!

My apologies if you received an update email 😵‍💫

Phainon stands alone at the edge of the seaside cliff. The sky is muddy, covered by a blanket of thick, grey clouds. He stares upwards, allowing the torrential downpour to pelt his face and sting his eyes.

In front of him is a crudely made grave. He dug the wet earth with his greatsword and when that didn’t work, his bare hands. The teddy bear now lies entombed, a final goodbye to the village, the innocent people he had failed to save. He hopes their souls are resting now, given a chance to find peace in the calm of the sea of flowers.  

He doesn’t know how long he’s been here, planted in the same place. The water has soaked through his thin robes, and the biting cold has long turned into a resounding numbness. The bruising on his thighs and the weeping gash in his chest no longer register. 

He feels nothing. Slowly, he moves closer to the edge of the cliff. 

Time stills. The rain continues to pelt his face. His wet clothing and wet wound wrappings stick to his body like a second skin. He prays and prays, begs over and over for a forgiveness that will never arrive. Yet again, he has survived when others have not, and he knows it's because the prophecy binds him. His fate is set in stone. 

Distracted by his racing thoughts and the resounding cold, he doesn’t notice the soft pitter patter of footsteps behind him. 

“There you are,” Mydei says. “I’ve been searching for you.”

Phainon doesn’t move, doesn’t turn to greet Mydei or respond. He continues to stare blankly at the sky. There’s no need to guess why the other man is here. He’s going to be reprimanded and questioned for his mistakes. 

“You should be resting,” Mydei continues. 

Oh, how he wants to. How he wishes he could fall unconscious and erase the images ravaging his mind, the memories that won’t leave him alone no matter what, the guilt over failing to save those who viewed him as their saving light. 

“They’re all gone now. The entire village, not a soul left,” Phainon mutters, more to himself than to Mydei. His fists clench on their own, fingernails digging into the tender flesh of his palm. 

“Deliverer,” Mydei says. 

That mocking nickname. Phainon bites his cheek as tears continue to drip down his chin. He can’t show his weakness, but the tremble of his figure betrays him.  

He laughs, well aware it sounds more like a strangled choke than anything else. No matter how hard he tries, the tears continue to fall, mixing with the rainwater wetting his cheeks. 

And he knows, if he were to turn back, Mydei would be staring back at him with those sharp eyes, slicing through him and picking apart the pieces. He would wear an expression of boredom, unbothered, unaffected by everything around him, the constant bloodshed and nonstop violence.

To a man like Mydei, he looks like a pitiful fool. A pathetic excuse for a so-called “hero”. He’s never felt like a hero, even if the title has been tattooed onto him by those in Okhema and Amphoreus at large. 

It hurts. Everything hurts. He wants to turn back time and return to when he was nothing more than a village boy gathering wheat in his arms. Back when he had everything, back when there was no prophecy etched permanently into his head. Back when he had his parents, his family, his friends. 

Back when he was himself.

He has nothing left, only memories seared into his head of his loved ones slain by his hand, of Cyrene’s chest bursting with gold ichor, stabbed to death by a strange spectre donning a mask and a black cloak. And now, the destruction of a small village that saw him as their savior. His appearance doomed them to a fate worse than death. 

“How can I be the hero to usher in a new era when I can’t even save a single child from being consumed by the black tide?” Phainon laughs brokenly. “How…” 

“Let’s go inside,” Mydei says softly. “You’ll catch a cold.”

Only then does he turn back to look at the other. Mydei, who’s as drenched as he is, telling him to go inside? But he sees those sharp golden eyes staring back at him. There’s none of that contempt or pity that he expects to see.

***

Phainon lays in bed while Mydei’s busy in the kitchen. The aroma of chicken and spices fills the room, comforting if it weren’t for the nausea building in the pit of his stomach. 

The room is silent aside from Mydei’s occasional movements and the sound of bubbling liquid on the stove. 

He drinks the soup given to him. The savoriness coats his tongue, and the bowl is warm in his icy hands. He hasn’t eaten all day, and it’s now he realizes how empty he feels, but his appetite is gone, and he can barely swallow. 

“It’s good,” Phainon says, refusing to make eye contact. “Didn’t know you could cook…” 

Mydei sits across from him. The table is small and so is the kitchen, barely a counter and a stove, but it’s enough. “I enjoy it when I am able.”

“I thought you ate your meat raw and drank blood,” Phainon murmurs. He stares blankly at his spoon.  

Mydei sighs. “Kremnoans did, once upon a time.” When Phainon doesn’t respond, he continues. “We drink pomegranate juice now.” 

“Is that what you always have in chalice..?” Phainon mumbles. “No wonder you like it so much…”

“Did you actually think I was drinking blood?” Mydei asks, incredulous. 

Phainon shrugs. “Maybe, maybe not.”

Warm savoriness coats his tongue as he takes another sip of the soup. For a few moments, it warms his body only to be overtaken by the numbing chill that has made its permanent home in his chest. He can’t stand staying here any longer. It’s a waste of time to be wallowing in this place instead of back at Okhema where he can be surrounded by disappointed faces and judgemental whisperings. He deserves the scorn. Dropping his spoon into the bowl with a clang, he says, “We’re done with the mission. We should get back to Okhema instead of wasting time. Aglaea needs to know we failed. The village we were sent to protect… is no more.”

Mydei shakes his head as he stares at Phainon. His expression remains a careful neutral. “I’ve already contacted her. We will stay another few days for you to heal your wounds. You are in no condition to head back.” 

“These wounds are nothing,” Phainon says. “Inconvenient, maybe, but I’ll survive.”

“We are staying a few more days.”

Phainon closes his eyes. Calm down , he tells himself. “What did Aglaea say? Was she disappointed?”

“She was worried about you and asked if you were okay.” 

“I’m fine,” Phainon responds flatly. 

“You are not.”

“I’m over my little outburst from earlier.” He forces himself up regardless of the screaming of his thighs and the sharp pain in his chest. His robes have half-dried, and it feels uncomfortable against his skin. “We should head back.” 

Mydei remains unwavering. “You are obviously not fine, and no, we will not.”

Phainon’s expression falls, tension set in his jaw. “Who are you to say if I feel fine or not?”

“It’s written all over your face, Deliverer.” As Mydei speaks, he tries to reach out.  

The name, that mocking accursed name sears itself into his head. Phainon snaps. His vision burns red, and he slaps the hand away. 

“Fuck you!” Phainon yells. “You barely know me and yet you speak to me like this! How can someone like you even begin to know how I feel?! We are going back to Okhema right this instant, and you can’t stop me!”

Mydei stays frozen in place. His eyes widen ever so slightly as he pulls his hand away. It falls slack to his side. 

“I’m sorry if I’m not some hardass like you are,” Phainon laughs. “I don’t live for this bloodshed. I can’t stop caring like you can. You may have no trouble razing through cities, but I… I can’t stand this…”

A spark of hurt flashes in those sharp golden eyes only to dissipate immediately. Phainon can’t say if he saw correctly or not, but he doesn’t care, not when he can barely think straight. It only pisses him off more, seeing how unbothered Mydei is, how he’s the only one making a ruckus while Mydei stays composed with not a single hair strand out of place.  

Pairing them together was a mistake. Aglaea should have known better. 

All they do is fight, that’s all there is to their relationship. They have nothing in common.

“No response?” Phainon laughs. “Your reputation precedes you, oh crown prince of Castrum Kremnos. I know what you’re capable of. I’ve heard the stories of how you ripped a man’s throat out with your bare hands and drank the blood that ran down your arm. You thrive off violence, find joy in needless suffering. We are nothing alike. You can’t even begin to understand how I feel. Don’t even try. It’s fine if you think I’m weak. I really don’t care anymore.” 

Mydei’s expression darkens. 

For a moment, there’s a tiny prickle of fear and a voice that screams at him that he’s made a terrible mistake. By prodding the lion, Phainon is now faced with its sharp fangs and even sharper claws. There’s only Mydei and him in this room. Though he knows he can hold his ground in a fight, he’s injured, and Mydei has the upper hand. But instead of allowing that fear to overtake him, Phainon grows angrier instead. He’ll fight Mydei in this small room if he has to, let his words and fists do the talking. He won’t take it lying down. 

Only Mydei doesn’t lash out. He remains calm as he stares down at his bowl of half-eaten soup. His lashes cast a deep shadow over his eyes and his voice comes out quiet, softer than his usual low timbre and somber in a way Phainon has never heard before. “The stories are true. I do not blame you for thinking of me in such a manner.”

Phainon narrows his eyes. His heart beats loudly and erratically.

“I remember that day as if it were yesterday.” Mydei stares down at his right hand, covered by his metal gauntlet and continues, “At the time, it was a triumphant victory. But now, I look back and realize how fragile yet precious life is.”

The regret is tangible on his face, and Phainon’s anger slowly morphs into confusion.

“I’ve made my fair share of mistakes that I will never again repeat. It took coming to Okhema to see the damage that Castrum Kremnos—no, I—have caused.” Mydei clenches his fist. “My homeland stands drenched in the blood of millions, innocents caught in the crossfire and warriors fighting for an honor that does not exist.”

Though he sounds genuine, still Phainon refuses to believe. “What made you change? It couldn’t have been Okhema only. You’ve been here for two months.”

“I’ve been nursing these thoughts long before my arrival at Okhema,” Mydei replies easily. “Surrounded by my countrymen who clamor for battle, I found myself believing in the destruction, saw it as something to be proud of, but I always had a sense of uneasiness I could not shake off.” 

“I see…” Phainon mutters, conflicted.

Mydei places his spoon in his empty bowl and stands up, his chair scraping against the creaky wooden floorboards. “I’ll leave you some space. It should be no trouble to ask the innkeeper for another room.”

At once, panic floods his senses. Phainon says, “No. Don’t go.”

“My presence upsets you. I rather—”

“Stay.” Phainon scrambles to reach over and grab Mydei’s wrist. “Please.”

Conflict brews, and for a moment, it seems Mydei wants to pull away. Phainon holds on tighter and stares with pleading eyes, begging almost. He doesn’t know what’s come over him, but he doesn’t want Mydei to leave. He doesn’t want to be left alone again. 

“Please.” 

Mydei purses his lips then sits back down. “Very well.” 

It’s silent once more. The air is thick, and Phainon is made aware of his every movement. The fire from before has fizzled out, and he’s left feeling even worse than before.

The prince continues as he always does, quiet and reserved. With his head tilted down, his expression is cast in deep shadow. He looks more forlorn than cold and brooding as Phainon had previously believed. 

“I’m sorry,” Phainon says softly. “You didn’t deserve that.”

With a shake of his head, Mydei says, “I’m used to it. This isn’t the first time I’ve had this conversation nor will it be the last.”

“But—”

“I don’t take any offense. Besides, this isn’t about me.” Mydei looks back up. His golden eyes are radiant, clear, and it makes Phainon’s breath hitch. “Contrary to what you may believe, I do care about you.”

“You’re only saying that to placate me,” Phainon responds, eyebrows furrowing. “I barely know you.”

“Even so, I believe in you,” Mydei says. It sounds so genuine that it has Phainon choking on air. He’s left hacking and coughing, making a mess of himself in front of the other as if he hasn’t done that enough already. 

He wipes at his lip and says, “I’m a nobody from a farming village that doesn’t exist anymore. I couldn’t save my friends or family or anyone for that matter. How could I possibly lead Amphoreus into a new era?”

“You will,” Mydei says. “Even if you don’t believe in yourself, the rest of us do.” 

“The only reason why I came to Okhema was for revenge,” Phainon challenges. “My intentions are not pure.”

Mydei clasps his hands together.  “They don’t have to be. Who says you need pure intentions?”

Phainon blinks. “A hero must have good intentions. The ones from myth—”

“Are assholes,” Mydei finishes. “Besides… you’re a good person. I haven’t known you for long, but I can ascertain your character.”

“You can’t be serious.” 

“I am.”

Phainon feels his throat close. “You can’t be.” 

“I know a good soul when I see one,” Mydei responds easily. “Believe in yourself more, Deliverer.”

“There goes that nickname again,” Phainon mutters. He’s being mocked. Again. 

“I call you that because I believe in you.” 

Liar. “You use it mockingly half the time,” Phainon shoots back. 

“You’re not wrong, but my point still stands,” Mydei says, steadfast.  

It’s hard to know what’s truth and what’s lies. Mydei believes in him? It has to be a joke. He has to be messing with him because why would he, after witnessing Phainon at his very worst, still have any trust? 

He should be met with scorn, not this… He doesn’t deserve this type of unrestrained kindness, especially not from someone as fearless and controlled as Mydei. 

But Mydei is not the type to lie or hide from the truth. That much Phainon knows. The prince is too straightforward for that sort of thing, honesty steeped in his every action. His words are deliberate, chosen, never out of a whim. 

“I wish I could be more like you. Not afraid of anything,” Phainon admits. The corner of his eyes ache once more. He doesn’t know what possesses him to say such secrets, but he needs to prove to Mydei that he’s not worthy. 

After all, Mydei is younger than him. A hard pill to swallow. Sometimes Phainon still can’t believe it. The look in the prince’s eyes is not one of youth. No, it’s one of a warrior worn down by the years gone by with not a single trace of that soft innocence so coveted. He wonders what Mydei looked like when he was young, if he ever held a gentle smile and danced freely beneath the open skies. 

He’s heard the stories, the prince scorned by his parents, thrown into the sea of souls to drown. It must be true. Phainon had believed it to be a myth, but when he’s faced with such a powerful presence, he finds his skepticism faltering. Mydei must have lived a horrific life thus far, yet… 

How is it that he can hold himself so strong? How is it that Phainon can’t? How is it that he’s so weak that he can’t even save a little girl? 

If only he hadn’t ignored the signs. If only he had been quicker. If only he hadn’t gotten so into his own head. 

“That’s not true. There is no word for ‘fear’ in the Kremnoan language, but I have felt it,” Mydei says slowly. The next words that leave his mouth have Phainon scrambling, expectation crumbling beneath his feet. “I don’t know what I’m doing either. I have, at many times, questioned my decisions. Even now… living in Okhema, following the flame-chase journey, I don’t know if I made the right choice.”

“You don’t seem that way,” Phainon says. He stares at Mydei, attempting to find any lies hidden within only to come up with nothing. “I’ve never seen you lose your cool.”

Mydei shakes his head. “I can’t afford to. Not when I have my people counting on me.” 

“Do you ever think about running away?” 

When the words leave his lips, Phainon immediately feels regret. Only a coward would think such thoughts, and Mydei is no coward. Phainon, well, he’s not sure where he stands. He wants to run, but where to? There’s nowhere he could hide behind even if he wanted to. 

“I have,” Mydei admits. He toys with his braid, his eyes downcast as he says, “It’s crossed my mind a few times in the past, how much easier it would be to lift the veil of responsibility and run away. I would not have to be responsible for so many, but…” He looks up at Phainon, his golden eyes blazing. “There is no dignity in such an existence. I did not choose my life, but it’s what I’ve been given, and I will ensure that the choices I make will carve out a better future for those that come after me. Never again shall the mistakes of the past repeat, not if I can stop it.” 

A better future. Phainon wants to laugh. He’s afraid of the future because he knows he will once again be left alone. He’s not daft. The prophecy is rather straightforward. 

Both the past and the future weigh on him. Even living in the present is difficult when the weight of expectation increases with each passing day. 

“I’ve taught myself to look away from the past, to not allow old memories to bind you and weigh you down,” Mydei says. “Keep moving on.”

“How?” Phainon whispers. The gash in his chest stings. “I try to but… all I can remember are the faces of those I’ve failed.”

Mydei nods. “I see them too sometimes. It’s difficult and can feel impossible, but the tides of time continue, flowers bloom and wither, the seasons change, and the cycle continues on. My time here is limited, the flame-chase journey dictates my future, but I will do as I can to carve out a path for myself and to bring hope to not only my people but all of Amphoreus… and to make up for the mistakes I’ve made before.”

Phainon allows the words to settle. He grasps for a response, but it slips through his fingers. 

“I do not mean to be brutal,” Mydei says gently. “But that is my view on the matter.” 

Mydei prepares them herbal tea, flavored sweet with honey. A delicacy of this region, fragrant and hearty, it warms his soul with every sip. 

***

The hot shower spray feels nice on his cold skin and aching muscles. He washes away the remaining grime, hissing slightly when the water makes contact with his wounds. It gives him precious time to think. 

He slips on a fresh chiton, courtesy of the inn. It doesn’t cover much, but it’s comfortable and already, he feels lighter. The anger from before has dissipated completely, and while he doesn’t feel good, he feels okay enough to function.

His racing thoughts have stilled. Only Mydei’s reassuring words circle in his mind as he ponders them over. He doesn’t think he’ll ever have the strength that Mydei does, but it’s comforting to know that he’s not alone in this. The uncertainty remains and will always remain, but that’s part of the journey ahead. 

Stepping out of the bathroom, Phainon suddenly comes to the realization that the inn room is insanely small. It’s barely big enough for one grown man, especially cramped for two. 

Mydei lounges on the seat in the corner of the room, right beside the singular bed that takes up nearly a third of the room. He has also rid himself of his armor, donning the same thin white chiton that leaves little to the imagination. Phainon has to look away before his mind starts running with ideas. 

“Let me help you with your bandages before you bleed through your spare clothing,” Mydei says. 

“It’s fine. I’ll walk around shirtless if I have to,” Phainon shrugs as approaches Mydei. He towels his hair in an attempt to distract himself as he forces himself to stare at Mydei’s face instead of his exposed body, the crimson of his red markings and the tempting sculpt of his chest. 

“Aglaea won’t be too happy to see her handiwork stained by carelessness,” Mydei continues, unaware of Phainon’s internal turmoil. “The other pair is already ruined.”

Phainon clicks his tongue. “You really know how to hit where it hurts, huh?”

Mydei smiles, if only a little. “Not my fault you act like a petulant child.”

“I’m older than you!” Phainon huffs. “By a decent amount, I may add.”

“Oh?” Mydei tilts his head. “Act your age then. I have no need to babysit a fully grown baby.”

“You’re lucky I’m injured right now.”

“Do you always resort to violence when you don’t get your way, Deliverer?” 

Phainon scoffs. “You of all people cannot be saying that.”

“Sit down,” Mydei says, pointing over at the bed. 

“Make me.” 

Mydei pushes him and Phainon resists, poking his tongue out. Little by little, he’s dragged to the edge of the bed and when he’s shoved down, he pulls Mydei with him. 

“What are you doing?” Mydei says, their chests pressed together and faces only centimeters apart. This close, he can see all of Mydei’s individual lashes and the flecks of orange in those golden eyes. 

It’s mesmerizing, and he finds he can’t look away. Without a second thought, Phainon wraps his arms around Mydei’s waist, trapping him. 

Mydei’s eyes widen, his composure gone as he tries to pull himself off. “You…! You’re injured—” 

“I’m fine,” Phainon says with a slight wince. The metal grooves of Mydei’s golden necklace dig into his skin and press against his wound, but he feels warmer than he has in ages. 

“Are you insane?” Mydei whispers, his eyes flicking down to where they’re so inappropriately connected.

“Maybe a little,” Phainon says as he grips on tighter. “Or a lot. Depends who you ask.”

“I’m hurting you,” Mydei says, his brows furrowed in concern. “At least let me help dress your wounds before they tear open even more. You’re bleeding again.”

“Mmm. You are rather heavy, I admit,” Phainon smiles. “What do I get as a prize if I let you?”

“You really are a spoiled child,” Mydei sighs.

“And you’re my babysitter,” Phainon says as he starts twirling Mydei’s braid around. “Though you’re not doing the greatest job. Passable, but not amazing. Aren’t you supposed to make sure I’m happy and well taken care of?”

“Hmph. You’re difficult to please.” Mydei’s eyes soften. “Very well. What is it you want?”

“Lay in bed with me after,” Phainon says. Only when Mydei nods does he reluctantly let go and allow Mydei to climb off him. 

“Sit up,” Mydei grumbles, his face a smidge redder than before, as he hooks two fingers beneath Phainon’s leather choker and yanks him up. He settles Phainon behind a bulk of pillows and huffs, “You were easier to deal with when you pointedly disliked me.” 

“I never disliked you,” Phainon coughs out as his cheeks burn. Oh. He’s never been pulled before by his choker. It’s definitely unlocked a part of him that he’s never thought about. 

“Could have had me fooled,” Mydei says as he procures some healing balm in a small metal tin. He slathers it on his fingers and warns, “It’ll burn a little.” 

“I wasn’t in the right state of mind,” Phainon admits, wincing slightly as Mydei dabs gently. The pain isn’t so bad, and he’s a little distracted by how gentle Mydei is and the lightness of his expression. “I’ve been needlessly cruel to you.”

“You are upset. It’s only natural,” Mydei says, his head tilted down, bangs covering his eyes, as he works on Phainon’s wound. “I do not fault you if you dislike me.”

“I don’t.”

Mydei silently wraps Phainon’s wound in bandages. He takes extra care to not jostle Phainon around too much and his wrappings are tidy from years of experience. With the chest bandages finished, he moves down to Phainon’s thighs, hidden beneath long flowing fabric. He pauses, hesitant to overstep.

“Go ahead,” Phainon says, ignoring the way his ears begin to burn. He could easily do it himself, but Mydei offered and who is he to refuse?

Mydei pushes the fabric away and slowly rubs the balm over the ring of thick, mottled bruises. The warmth of his gentle touch feels nice if Phainon can ignore the way his heart rings in his chest. Each tentative touch is a flame lit.

“I should have been with you the entire time,” Mydei says, his voice barely above a whisper. “This wouldn’t have happened had I not left.” 

“It’s not your fault. We both agreed to split ground,” Phainon says as he reaches out to play with Mydei’s golden earring. Mydei’s face scrunches up. 

The massage feels nice and the healing balm tingles. Mydei works efficiently and his head stays bowed down. It’s a little strange to be in this position, having a prince service him like this. 

In the dim light of their shared inn room, the world narrows to only the two of them. Mydei’s hands are calloused but warm and Phainon wants so badly to reach out and lock their fingers together. A rather inappropriate thought on his end, but he doesn’t care. Knowing that Mydei does indeed care for him, that it’s very possible for their relationship to extend further than battle, has Phainon grinning wider than he has in months. 

“Done,” Mydei says. “How do you feel?” 

“Good,” Phainon replies cheerily as he fluffs up pillows and lays down on his back. He pats the empty area beside him and says, “My reward?”

When they finally make their way back to Okhema, Aglaea is already waiting at the gates for them. 

“Welcome back,” she says gently, her lovely voice like a blossom floating in the breeze. “We have much to discuss.”

Phainon tenses, his blood freezing over like a lake in winter, only to relax when Mydei places a gentle hand on his shoulder. The warmth, the grounding gesture melts away the tension, and when he sees the barest quirk of a smile, an earnest attempt to reassure, his heart skips a beat. 

It’ll be okay, Deliverer, he can hear Mydei saying.

The meeting with Aglaea goes better than he expects, even though he does try to argue when she tells them that they’ve done their best, and if she notices them standing a little closer than on opposite sides, she doesn’t say a word.

***

For the next few days, Phainon stays in his room. His injuries have mostly healed over thanks to Hyacine’s magic, but he doesn’t feel normal, unable to leave the confines of his self-imposed prison, unable to brave the dawn that Kephale has blessed upon Okhema. 

His sleep has been horrific. The dreams return stronger than ever melding with the recent events. It’s almost funny how he believed he had grown stronger, only to be brought back to reality. He wishes for the warmth of the body beside him, a warmth he’s grown used to in the past few days. 

But, no. He can’t bother Mydei anymore. They’re back in Okhema, and Mydei has his duties and his responsibilities to his people. 

It’s fine. He can wait. They’re on far better terms now. That at least is a comfort, even if he’s nursing these feelings that won’t go away regardless of how hard he tries to rid himself of them. 

Maybe when Mydei settles down completely will Phainon go and bother him with yet another competition. Maybe he’ll be able to kiss Mydei again and have his body slotted nicely against his own.

He falls back into another fitful sleep only to be woken up by a sharp rap at his front door. 

“Mydei,” Phainon greets, internally panicking as he pats himself down to look a little more presentable. He’s in his sleeping robes, thin and loose, and his hair is a bird’s nest, sticking in all different directions. It’s probably not working, there’s only so much he can smooth out. He knows he looks like a mess.

“Deliverer.” Mydei greets, and Phainon feels his sore muscles automatically loosen at the sound of the familiar, deep voice only to tense up when Mydei continues with, “Hyacine revealed to me your habits. Give them up.”

“No, how are you? How have you been? It’s nice to see you? Nothing?” Phainon laughs. He’s tempted to slam his door in Mydei’s face, but the prince has already slotted his foot between the door in anticipation of such a reaction. 

“Deliverer,” Mydei says. His voice takes a tone of warning, though the soft edges show concern rather than threat. 

“Yes? I do believe you’re breaching my privacy. I’ll have to speak to Hyacine about letting others know about what I do in my free time,” Phainon says.

“Those pills are not regulated. They’re terrible for you. Are you aware of the side effects?”

Phainon rolls his eyes. “You really think I don’t know?”

“Give them,” Mydei says, pushing himself into Phainon’s house. “I’ll rummage through everything if I have to.” 

Before Mydei starts tearing a hole in his space, Phainon admits, “I don’t have any more. I brought the last of my batch to the mission and well, you know how that turned out.”

Mydei pauses. “Is that why you have sunken eyebags and look horrifically pale?” 

“You sure know how to let someone off easy,” Phainon laughs. 

“I didn’t mean to insult.”

Phainon smiles. He’s gotten a better grasp of Mydei’s habits by now, how he scrunches his nose a little if he’s upset or how he idly plays with his braid as a source of comfort. 

“You can look all you want but you won’t find anything,” Phainon says as he scoots over to the fridge. “Do you want anything to drink?” 

“I’m fine.” Conflict brews in Mydei’s golden eyes, and he opens his mouth to say something only to close it. He looks a little lost but then he says, “You seemed to sleep okay before we made it back to Okhema.”

Phainon nearly chokes. Yeah. Because they spent most of the time cuddling and sleeping together in the same bed. And well, Phainon can try to deny it all he wants, hide himself away and act as if it’s all a coincidence, but these past few days have shown him it’s anything but that. 

“Do you know why?” Phainon asks, ignoring the faint flush creeping up his face. 

“I can guess.” Mydei tucks a stray strand of hair behind his ear and says, “If you wish, I can warm your bed.” 

Phainon chokes again. “Are you even hearing yourself?! You can’t just say that!”

“Is it not true?” Mydei challenges. “You clung onto me and slept like a baby.”

“I see what you’re playing at.” Phainon narrows his eyes. “Trying to pass off your own desires as a means to help me.”

“I came to see how you were doing, Deliverer. We can’t have your health deteriorating over black market drugs,” Mydei shoots back. He, too, is starting to grow a little red, and Phainon delights in it. Ha, he’s not as unaffected as he tries to seem. 

“And if I refuse?” 

“Then I will take my leave. I will only offer this once. Be warned, I will make sure you never get your hands on those pills ever again.” 

“You’re cruel you know that?” Phainon pouts.

“I’m effective,” Mydei corrects. 

Phainon steps closer, his heart pounding fast against his chest. The adrenaline rush gives him the push to say, “You know… I could potentially be persuaded with a kiss.” 

Mydei scoffs. He strides forward until they're nearly pressed chest to chest with only the barest sliver of space separating them. His voice takes a slight tone of amusement. “I don’t think you’re in a position to bargain, Deliverer.” 

They’re so close, so very close. Phainon could easily close the distance, could crash their bodies together and give Mydei no room to escape. He’s well aware Mydei is taunting him, testing him. The self-assured expression on his face speaks volumes. 

Phainon wraps his arms around Mydei’s waist. “Is that a yes?”

Instead of an answer, Mydei flicks him on the forehead. 

“Hey!” Phainon cries out, indignant. “Your gauntlet is sharp, you know!”

“I know,” Mydei smiles. 

Their faces are only millimeters apart, breaths mingling. Blue meets gold. Phainon leans forward and captures Mydei’s lips once more.
